templates.pattern: A cell is observed under a microscope. The image size is [IMG] mm and the actual size of the cell is [ACT] mm. Calculate the magnification of the microscope.
templates.explanation:
Magnification = image size ÷ actual size
= [IMG] ÷ [ACT]
= [RESULT]

Magnification tells us how many times larger the image appears compared to the real object. Light microscopes typically magnify up to ×1500 and electron microscopes up to ×500,000.

templates.pattern: A cell appears [IMG] mm in size under a microscope with a magnification of ×[MAG]. Calculate the actual size of the cell in mm.
templates.explanation:
Actual size = image size ÷ magnification
= [IMG] ÷ [MAG]
= [RESULT] mm

Always divide the image size by the magnification to find the actual size. Use consistent units throughout — convert all measurements to the same unit first.

templates.pattern: A cell has an actual size of [ACT] μm. It is viewed under a microscope with magnification ×[MAG]. Calculate the size of the image in μm.
templates.explanation:
Image size = actual size × magnification
= [ACT] × [MAG]
= [RESULT] μm

Multiply the actual size by the magnification to find the image size. A 10 μm cell at ×400 magnification appears 4000 μm = 4 mm in the image.

templates.pattern: A cubic cell has a side length of [L] μm. Calculate the total surface area of the cell in μm².
templates.explanation:
Surface area of cube = 6 × L²
= 6 × [L]²
= 6 × [L*L]
= [RESULT] μm²

A cube has 6 faces each with area L². Surface area determines the rate of exchange of substances — oxygen, nutrients and waste — with the environment.

templates.pattern: A cubic cell has a side length of [L] μm. Calculate the volume of the cell in μm³.
templates.explanation:
Volume of cube = L³
= [L]³
= [L] × [L] × [L]
= [RESULT] μm³

Volume determines the metabolic demand of a cell — larger cells need more nutrients and produce more waste. Volume increases faster than surface area as cell size increases.

templates.pattern: A cubic cell has a side length of [L] μm. Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of the cell in μm⁻¹.
templates.explanation:
SA:V ratio = 6L² ÷ L³ = 6 ÷ L
= 6 ÷ [L]
= [RESULT] μm⁻¹

As cell size increases SA:V ratio decreases. Small cells have high SA:V ratios allowing efficient exchange. Large cells struggle to exchange substances quickly enough — this limits maximum cell size.

templates.pattern: A single cell undergoes [N] rounds of cell division. Calculate the total number of cells produced.
templates.explanation:
Cells after n divisions = 2ⁿ
= 2^[N]
= [RESULT]

Each cell division doubles the number of cells. After 10 divisions one cell becomes 1024 cells. This exponential growth is important in development and tumour growth.

templates.pattern: A cell divides every [T] hours. Calculate the total time taken for [N] cell divisions in hours.
templates.explanation:
Total time = number of divisions × time per division
= [N] × [T]
= [RESULT] hours

Division time varies enormously — bacteria divide every 20 minutes, human cells every 24 hours. Cancer cells often divide faster than normal cells.

templates.pattern: A culture starts with [INITIAL] cells and grows to [FINAL] cells. Calculate the number of cell divisions that occurred.
templates.explanation:
Number of divisions = log₂(final ÷ initial)
= log₂([FINAL] ÷ [INITIAL])
= log₂([FINAL/INITIAL])
= [RESULT]

Each division doubles the population. Knowing the initial and final cell counts allows us to calculate exactly how many divisions occurred.
